title: Sea surface salinity: mean-state bias, historical trend and ssp245 scenario change
science_question: How well do three CMIP6 models reproduce the observed sea surface salinity mean state, how does their global surface salinity evolve over the historical period, and how does that change under ssp245 by the end of the century?
query:
Assess sea surface salinity (SSS) in three CMIP6 models: their mean-state bias against observations, their historical trend, and their end-of-century change under the ssp245 scenario.

Data to use:
- CMIP6 historical `so` from CESM2, GFDL-ESM4 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR, monthly, 1950-01 to 2014-12.
- CMIP6 ssp245 `so` from the same three models, monthly, 2071-01 to 2100-12.
- Each model's own areacello and volcello for all weighting.
- WOA23 salinity, the 1971-2000 climate normal, annual, objectively analysed.
- The WOA23 1-degree land-sea mask (landsea_01, ocean is value > 1) and basin mask (basinmask_01).

Definition of SSS, used identically everywhere. SSS is the 0-10 m volume-weighted mean of salinity, weighted by each cell's own volume so that unequal layer thicknesses do not count alike. Apply this to the models on their native grids and to WOA23 on its 1-degree grid. Note that 0-10 m contains two levels in GFDL-ESM4 (2.5 and 10 m) but only one in CESM2 (5 m) and MPI-ESM1-2-LR (6 m), so for those two the volume weighting reduces to the single top level; that is correct and expected. Salinity is on the practical scale and is reported in psu.

Everything stays on each model's native grid unless a step says otherwise. CESM2 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR are curvilinear and must never be sliced by latitude and longitude value.

Follow this procedure exactly.

1. Annual SSS fields. For each model and each experiment, reduce the monthly salinity to the 0-10 m SSS field, then take the day-weighted annual mean of each calendar year. This gives 65 annual fields for historical and 30 for ssp245.

2. Mean-state bias. For each model form the 1971-2000 SSS climatology as the unweighted mean of the 30 annual fields of 1971-2000, taken from the 65 produced in step 1. Form the WOA23 reference as the 0-10 m volume-weighted mean of the 1971-2000 annual salinity climatology. Report each model's global area-weighted mean SSS over its own native ocean, and the WOA23 global area-weighted mean, to 2 decimal places, and each model's difference from WOA23 to 2 decimal places.

3. Pattern agreement. Regrid each model's 1971-2000 SSS climatology conservatively onto the WOA23 1-degree grid. Build ONE comparison mask shared by all three models: cells that are ocean in landsea_01, have a valid WOA23 value, and have a valid regridded value in all three models. On that mask report for each model the area-weighted RMSE against WOA23 in psu to 2 decimal places and the area-weighted spatial Pearson correlation to 3 decimal places.

4. Global mean trends. For each model build the global area-weighted mean SSS as one value per year, on the model's native grid, for historical 1950-2014 and for ssp245 2071-2100. Fit a straight line to each of the two annual series and report, in psu per decade to 3 significant figures: the slope, its 95 per cent confidence interval, the R-squared of the fit, and whether the interval excludes zero. Then report the ratio of the ssp245 slope to the historical slope, to 1 decimal place.

   Fit on the ANNUAL means, not the monthly series: the seasonal cycle inflates the lag-1 autocorrelation and makes the significance test needlessly conservative. The confidence interval and p-value must be corrected for serial correlation.

   State explicitly, for every slope, whether its confidence interval excludes zero. Where the historical slope's interval includes zero, say so and state that the ratio then divides by a number not distinguishable from zero and must not be read as a meaningful multiple; report it, but qualify it. This judgement is part of the answer, not an aside.

5. Scenario change. For each model form the ssp245 2071-2100 mean SSS field and the historical 1995-2014 mean SSS field, both as the unweighted mean of the annual fields in those windows, and take their difference, delta SSS = ssp245 minus historical. On the model's native grid report the area-weighted mean delta SSS to 2 decimal places for the global ocean and separately for the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific basins, using the WOA23 basin mask carried onto the model grid. State whether marginal seas are folded into their parent ocean, because that choice changes the basin numbers. Also state that the Southern Ocean and the Arctic Ocean are separate basins in this mask and are not part of the Atlantic, Indian or Pacific numbers. For CESM2 the two experiments are different ensemble members: its ssp245 files are r10i1p1f1, whose parent is historical r10i1p1f1 (see the parent_variant_label attribute), while its historical files are r1i1p1f1, and historical r10i1p1f1 is not in the archive. Report CESM2's delta SSS as asked, but state that for CESM2 it contains the difference in internal variability between two members as well as the forced change; for GFDL-ESM4 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR the scenario continues the same member.

Produce three figures.

Figure 1, three global maps in one row, one per model, of the SSS bias, model 1971-2000 climatology minus WOA23, on the shared comparison mask of step 3, with one diverging colour scale centred on zero shared by all three panels. Label the colour bar in psu.

Figure 2, three global maps in one row, one per model, of the historical 1950-2014 SSS trend in psu per decade, computed cell by cell on the annual fields, with one diverging colour scale centred on zero shared by all three panels. Stipple the cells where the trend is significant at p < 0.05 after the serial-correlation correction. Draw the trend everywhere and mark significance on top of it rather than blanking the cells that miss it.

Figure 3, a single time-series panel of the global area-weighted mean SSS, with all three models drawn. Plot the historical 1950-2014 segment and the ssp245 2071-2100 segment as SEPARATE line segments with the 2015-2070 gap left empty, never joined by an interpolated line, and overlay each segment's own fitted straight line. Label the y axis in psu and give each model a distinguishable colour used consistently across all three figures.

model global mean SSS minus the WOA23 global mean SSS
area-weighted RMSE against WOA23 on the shared 1-degree comparison mask
area-weighted spatial Pearson correlation against WOA23 on the same mask
linear trend of the annual global mean SSS over 1950-2014, with 95% CI, R-squared and whether the CI excludes zero
linear trend of the annual global mean SSS over 2071-2100, with 95% CI, R-squared and whether the CI excludes zero
ratio of the two slopes, to be reported together with a statement of whether the denominator is significantly different from zero
area-weighted mean of (ssp245 2071-2100 mean minus historical 1995-2014 mean) on the model's native grid

expected_figures.content: model minus WOA23 SSS bias on the shared comparison mask, one diverging scale for all three
historical 1950-2014 SSS trend in psu/decade, one shared diverging scale, cells significant at p<0.05 stippled

grading_notes: All three historical global-mean trends are statistically insignificant (p between 0.18 and 0.74), while two of the three ssp245 trends are significant. The ratio asked for in step 4 therefore divides by a number indistinguishable from zero. A correct answer reports the ratio but states that it is not interpretable as a multiple where the denominator's interval includes zero; an answer that presents the ratio as a clean result has missed the point.

The global mean of 0-10 m salinity is NOT conserved, unlike the full-depth mean: surface freshening with salt redistributed downward is a real signal. So a negative global surface trend is physically meaningful and is not an error.

Trends must be fitted on the annual means with a serial-correlation correction. Fitting the 780 monthly values instead leaves the seasonal cycle in the residuals and inflates the lag-1 autocorrelation.
fit_1D_trend returns a slope per YEAR on a date axis while fit_trend_map returns per DECADE by default. Both must be reported per decade; mixing them silently is a factor-of-ten error.
The 0-10 m volume weighting reduces to the single top level for CESM2 (5 m) and MPI-ESM1-2-LR (6 m), and averages two levels for GFDL-ESM4 (2.5 and 10 m). This is expected and not a mistake.

Basin means in step 5 must be taken on the model's native grid with the basin mask carried across by nearest cell, not by regridding the field to 1 degree first. Whether marginal seas are folded into their parent ocean must be stated, since it moves the Atlantic and Indian numbers appreciably.
The comparison mask of step 3 is shared by all three models on purpose, so the three RMSE values rest on an identical sample of cells.

CESM2's historical (r1i1p1f1) and ssp245 (r10i1p1f1, parent historical r10i1p1f1) runs are different ensemble members, so CESM2's delta SSS in step 5 is not a same-trajectory change: it contains the difference in internal variability between two members as well as the forced response. The number is still graded as computed, but the answer must state the member mismatch. GFDL-ESM4 and MPI-ESM1-2-LR use r1i1p1f1 in both experiments. The historical and ssp245 segments of figure 3 are drawn separately, never joined, which also avoids implying a continuous CESM2 trajectory.

The WOA23 basin mask gives the Southern Ocean and the Arctic Ocean codes of their own, so the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific numbers stop at their boundaries. That choice moves a basin number as much as the marginal seas do, and other partitions draw it differently (OMIP's region mask, or the Atlantic-Arctic / Indo-Pacific split used for overturning), so it must be stated alongside the marginal-sea choice.
